summary: For ages 6-7, teach the commutative property of addition structurally: the same two amounts combine to the same whole whichever order they are taken (3+8 = 8+3), then exploit this to count on from the larger addend. Deliberately contrast subtraction (5−3 ≠ 3−5) so children do not over-generalise 'you can swap them'. The core insight is invariance (the addition total holds under reordering) versus change (the subtraction result shifts), and children should justify why, not just recite a rule.
misconceptions: Over-generalising to subtraction (thinking 5−3 = 3−5) — the key error this topic must pre-empt.
Treating a+b and b+a as different facts to learn separately.
Believing the answer changes with order because the counting process feels different.
Applying 'swap them' to word problems where order encodes meaning (start/change).
Not using commutativity strategically (counting on from the smaller number, doing more work).

activities.title: Swap bench: watch the addition total hold
steps: Combine two bars or rods — one of 3 and one of 8 — into a single total bar, and note the total (11).
Swap the two parts so 8 comes first and 3 second, and check whether the total bar's length changes.
On a number line, trace 8 then count on 3, and separately 3 then count on 8, and mark where each lands.
Say aloud what stayed the same and what moved: the parts traded places but the whole did not change.
Switch to subtraction: build 5 then remove 3, then try 3 then remove 5, and describe what happens when you try to take 5 from 3.
activities.insight: Reordering the two addends rearranges the parts but leaves the whole unchanged, so a+b = b+a; subtraction starts from one amount and removes the other, so swapping changes what you begin with and the result changes.

activities.title: Count on from the bigger number
steps: Given 3+8, decide which number to start from so there is less counting on to do, and explain your choice.
Count on from the larger addend to reach the total, then check against counting on from the smaller to confirm they agree.
Try 2+9: say which order you would count on from and why.
State the matching fact instantly: if you know 8+3, say 3+8 without recounting.
activities.insight: Because order does not change an addition total, you can always start from the larger number and count on the smaller one, which takes fewer steps (unless the two numbers are equal, as in 6+6) — commutativity is a calculation-saving strategy, and knowing one fact gives you its partner.

activities.title: Convince me: why addition swaps but subtraction doesn't
steps: Argue why 3+8 must equal 8+3, using a drawing or a rearrangement of objects rather than just asserting the rule.
Test whether the same swap works for take-away: predict, then model 8−5 and 5−8 with counters and report what happens.
Consider 6+6: does order matter here, and what does that tell you about the rule?
State in your own words which operation can be reordered and why the other cannot.
activities.insight: Addition combines the same two amounts whichever order you take them, so the whole is unchanged; subtraction removes one amount from another, so swapping changes the starting amount and the result. Justifying this builds reasoning beyond recall.

activities.title: True/false and matching checks
steps: Decide whether statements are true or false: is 3+8 = 8+3? is 5−3 = 3−5?
Match each addition to its swapped partner that gives the same total.
Choose which order is easier to count on from for a given sum, and say why.
activities.insight: Addition statements hold when the order is swapped; subtraction statements do not. Recognising this consolidates the distinction and the strategic use of counting on from the larger number.

checkQuestion: I know that 8 + 5 = 13. So what is 5 + 8? And does the same trick work for taking away — do 8 − 5 and 5 − 8 give the same answer? Tell me why.
checkAnswer: 5 + 8 = 13 (the same, because order doesn't change an addition). But 8 − 5 and 5 − 8 are NOT the same: 8 − 5 = 3, while 5 − 8 cannot be done with these counters / goes below zero. Reason: addition combines the same two amounts whichever order you take them; subtraction starts from one amount and removes the other, so swapping changes what you begin with.
